candidato.titulo: Managing high blood pressure could prevent >500K CVD deaths annually in 20 countries
candidato.resumo: Effective management of high blood pressure could prevent more than 518,000 annual deaths from cardiovascular disease around the world, according to preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Hypertension Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting is in Arlington, Virginia, Oct. 7–11, 2026, and focuses on recent advances in basic and clinical research on high blood pressure and its relationship to cardiac and kidney disease, stroke, obesity and genetics.

texto_fonte:
Managing high blood pressure could prevent >500K CVD deaths annually in 20 countries
Effective management of high blood pressure could prevent more than 518,000 annual deaths from cardiovascular disease around the world, according to preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Hypertension Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting is in Arlington, Virginia, Oct. 7–11, 2026, and focuses on recent advances in basic and clinical research on high blood pressure and its relationship to cardiac and kidney disease, stroke, obesity and genetics.
Untreated high blood pressure can cause blood vessel damage, including narrowing of the arteries and aneurysms, and lead to many heart conditions, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, enlarged left heart and metabolic syndrome. High blood pressure is the most prevalent and modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease and can affect adults in all age groups. Based on the American Heart Association's 2025 Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults, the treatment goal for adults with hypertension is less than 130/80 mm Hg.
Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are responsible for roughly three out of five deaths globally, and approximately 73% of these deaths occur in low- or middle-income countries. Cardiovascular disease accounts for more of these deaths than other chronic health conditions such as diabetes, cancers and chronic respiratory illnesses.
"In this study, we analyzed existing data to assess if expanding use of NCD preventive health care services across 20 countries worldwide could reduce cardiovascular deaths. We found that expanding treatment of high blood pressure to more people prevented the most deaths, followed by broader use of statin medications for high cholesterol and managing blood sugar in people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes," said Scott Pilla, MD, MHS, an associate professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore.
"While there were substantial gaps in the use of preventive health care services for these conditions in all countries, lower-middle-income countries had large opportunities for improvement, with low rates of hypertension control and high cholesterol management and minimal use of cancer screening tests."
Key findings include:
- The modeling analysis estimated that increasing preventive care services across the 20 upper- and lower-middle-income countries in the study from current levels to match the levels in high-performing U.S. health systems—approximately 80% of eligible patients—could prevent 518,476 annual cardiovascular deaths through hypertension control, 340,682 through treatment with statins when indicated and 309,520 through glucose control. Increasing colon cancer screening to 80% could prevent 206,767 colon cancer-related deaths each year.
- Improving blood pressure control prevented the greatest number of deaths of any preventive service, especially in upper-middle-income countries (223,282 annual deaths) and lower-middle-income countries (223,655 annual deaths).
- The modeling estimates found that only about one in five adults with hypertension in the 20 studied countries had controlled blood pressure (lower than 140/90 mm Hg). Similarly, 16% of individuals with high cholesterol levels used statins; 39% with type 1 or type 2 diabetes had blood sugar below optimal levels; and 14%–26% underwent routinely indicated cancer screenings.
- Among cancer screening methods, colon cancer screening prevented the most deaths, followed by cervical and breast cancer screening, respectively.
"This modeling analysis offers important information on the potential global impact of high blood pressure and, importantly, the opportunity to reduce the number of deaths due to high blood pressure-related conditions with treatment. Previous research has confirmed that following the evidence-based recommendations in the latest guideline can reduce the risk of death from high blood pressure and also reduce the risk of other serious conditions, such as heart failure, stroke and dementia," said chair of the American Heart Association's 2025 guideline writing committee Daniel W. Jones, MD, FAHA.
"Treatment of high blood pressure to goal leads to longer lives and also healthier lives. This study should inspire clinicians and patients to give more attention to appropriate management of high blood pressure using both lifestyle measures and medication." Jones, who was not involved in this study, is also a past volunteer president of the American Heart Association (2007–2008) and is dean and professor emeritus of the University of Mississippi School of Medicine in Jackson, Mississippi.

candidato.titulo: Zimbabwe's dinosaurs were different from South Africa's: New species offers clues
candidato.resumo: Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth's animal and plant species. This diversity is driven by varied habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for nearly two centuries.

texto_fonte:
Zimbabwe's dinosaurs were different from South Africa's: New species offers clues
Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth's animal and plant species. This diversity is driven by varied habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for nearly two centuries.
Africa is most famous for spectacular hominid fossils that reveal our own ancestry. However, the continent boasts many fabulous fossil finds, including those of the most familiar extinct animals—dinosaurs.
The first African dinosaur fossils to be noted scientifically hailed from the Eastern Cape, South Africa, and were described in the 1850s. Since then, the African dinosaur map has expanded, with rich fossil beds in South Africa, Lesotho, Tanzania, Egypt, Niger, Malawi, Madagascar and Morocco.
Zimbabwe is an important part of the African dinosaur puzzle, with dinosaur bones reported since 1916.
As a specialist on early dinosaurs who has worked on similar material from China, the U.K. and Africa, I've been drawn to these Zimbabwean fossils to see what they reveal about the first stages of dinosaur evolution.
Our latest addition to the Triassic zoo, Musango matusadonaensis, is a sauropodomorph dinosaur. (That's the dinosaur subgroup that eventually gave rise to four-legged, long-necked giants like Diplodocus.)
Its incomplete skeleton was found in the bank of the Nyamasango River close to Musango Island, as captured in the animal's scientific name. Musango's anatomy shows us that it was bipedal (walking on its hind legs only), reached about 4.5 meters (15 feet) in length and weighed 220 kilograms (485 pounds). Growth marks in its bones reveal that it was a subadult when it died. Sadly, the skull wasn't preserved, so its diet is unknown, but its close relatives were largely herbivorous (plant-eating).
Our new work reveals something unexpected about Zimbabwean dinosaurs. They're not simply an extension of better-known South African faunas but include an array of species unique to the region. We're now trying to work out why these differences exist. We suspect that environmental conditions might be the key.
The search
Early fossil finds in Zimbabwe were overlooked by many scientists, and it was not until the 1970s that they became more generally known. This was thanks to pioneering work by Zimbabwean paleontologists Geoffrey Bond and Michael Raath, who discovered abundant material in the hinterlands of Bulawayo (southwestern Zimbabwe) and the lower Zambezi Valley (forming the border with Zambia). Most of these finds were identified as belonging to known species named from neighboring South Africa.
Paleontological work in Zimbabwe stalled for a few decades. However, a band of devoted fossil hunters kept searching. One of them, Steve Edwards, a local safari camp manager, found new, productive sites on the shore of Lake Kariba, the artificial lake that forms most of the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia.
News of the discoveries eventually reached Jonah Choiniere at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. Choiniere, an expert on early dinosaurs, immediately recognized the importance of the material. He assembled an international team of collaborators from South Africa, Zimbabwe and the U.K. to explore the sites further.
This was a major task, as the sites on Lake Kariba's shoreline are deep inside Matusadona National Park. Our solution was to use one of the Kariba houseboats as a mobile hotel and laboratory so that we could prospect the shoreline. We mounted two expeditions, in 2017 and 2018. We have been cleaning and studying this material ever since.
Both trips yielded a trove of material, collected from brick-red mudstones and sandstones that were laid down by ancient rivers around 210 million years ago, during the Late Triassic period (237–201 million years ago). Geological evidence and plant fossils show that the Triassic landscape of Kariba was dry and dotted with stands of large conifer trees, with green corridors of vegetation following permanent watercourses.
What's unique
Sauropodomorphs are the most common Late Triassic dinosaurs. But what's interesting about Musango and its relative Musankwa (which we described from the same beds in 2024) is that they are unique to Zimbabwe.
We'd expected to find South African dinosaur species in these beds, given their similar age and geographic proximity, but surprisingly, all the material we've collected so far has revealed animals that are distinct from those elsewhere.
These Zimbabwean dinosaurs are not even the closest relatives of their South African neighbors. We've also found other fossil animals, including lungfish and aquatic reptiles called phytosaurs, which are rare or absent in South African sites.
Following this, we've started to reappraise the historical dinosaur collections in Bulawayo. It appears that many of these fossils can't be assigned to South African species either, contrary to earlier assumptions.
Then, as now, Zimbabwe was farther north than South Africa and closer to the equator, so climatic differences might be responsible for these varied casts of characters (as climate is known to have a strong effect on the distributions of living animals). To probe this further, we'll be going back to Kariba in search of more fossils.
We'll also collect more information on the exact ages and environments of these dinosaur-bearing rocks to compare them more precisely with sites elsewhere. Although the significance of these dinosaurs is only just coming to light, Zimbabwe is already taking a greater role in shedding much-needed light on early dinosaur evolution.

candidato.titulo: Will ‘boring’ robots win in the real world? Why robotic form should follow workflow
candidato.resumo: If we want to move physical AI from social media feeds to a sustained commercial level, we must reverse our current approach. The post Will ‘boring’ robots win in the real world? Why robotic form should follow workflow appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Robots have captured our imagination. We have seen humanoids balancing on one leg, doing backflips, folding laundry, and moving smoothly over difficult terrain. This is all behavior that only a few years ago seemed like something out of science fiction. These viral examples matter because they show that embodied AI has reached a new technical stage.
At the same time, the window on what qualifies as a “humanoid robot” seems to be shifting. Robot companies are adding wheels, more sensors, new manipulators, hats, and screens, while they take away eyes and heads from their humanoid robot designs.
As an engineering ecosystem working directly alongside humanoid developers to solve core hardware bottlenecks, we see a recurring theme. The industry frequently gets caught up in “robot-forward” thinking. We build an extraordinary physical platform first, then scour industrial sites for a task for it to perform.
If we want to move physical AI from social media feeds to a sustained commercial level, we must reverse our current approach. The industry needs a design method that works backwards from the workflow. Begin with a task that has economic value. Consider whether a robot can carry out that task better than a human can.
Then, go backwards to find out exactly what hardware, sensing capabilities, and form factor are actually needed to carry out the task.
The sensor stack is born in the task, not the datasheet
If you start by designing a platform, you will likely end up with a compromised hardware stack. The specific workflow determines the machine’s engineering requirements.
Let’s take as an example a bipedal humanoid robot that is asked to carry out two different industrial work processes. One involves inserting a pin on an automotive assembly line and the other involves packing a pallet in a logistics center.
A pin connector insertion task generally involves a 20 µm clearance and 5 N mating force. So, there needs to be contact-force resolution below 0.1 N and a control bandwidth fast enough to detect jamming before a sensitive pin bends.
Yet, when using the same arm for bulk pallet packing, you need almost none of that high-frequency micro-force resolution. Instead, you need heavy payload capacity, structural rigidity, and the ability to endure 1 million cycles without baseline mechanical drift.
If you are building a general-purpose platform, a single “middle-of-the-road” force sensor may result in a system that could make precise pin insertion difficult. The system could also lack the durability needed for continuous heavy lifting.
The workflow also determines your error budget. This is the only factor that turns force sensing from a cost item into something that provides a demonstrable return on investment.
Attempts to improve force sensing often fail. For example, our tests have shown that using a specific calculation maintaining contact force at ±0.2 N, can reduce connector scrap in amounts from 1.2% to 0.5%. This can translate into annual estimated savings of approximately $450,000 per assembly line. This kind of economic argument is only possible if you begin with the task in question.
That is exactly the reason why the selection of critical components, for example those based on strain sensing, must take place at the architectural design stage rather than being treated as an afterthought when preparing the bill of materials (BOM).
Adjusting the robot rather than adjusting the facility
The tendency to focus on the task first raises the main question about form factor. Is a specialised form factor the better choice? When is a humanoid design strictly necessary?
Operating environments can be divided into two types: greenfield and brownfield. The real issue is not what the robot should look like, but whether it is cheaper to modify the robot or to modify the facility.
With greenfield sites, you can use specialized robots. With brownfield sites, like an existing refinery or chemical plant, the robot has to adapt to spaces created for humans.
In greenfield builds, like Equinor’s Northern Lights facility, the operator can design the layout from the beginning and construct the facility around the task. So, specialized, non-humanoid forms almost always prove better in terms of unit economics, speed, and energy efficiency. Legged and wheeled robots are more reliable for the types of tasks they carry out.
However, in most cases, industrial activities take place in brownfield sites, where the only practical option is to adapt the existing platform. These sites have narrow aisles, stairs, floor grating, and doorways designed with the human body in mind. In this situation, a human-suitable form factor, whether that involves legs, two arms, or a humanoid shape, becomes a major advantage. It lets the equipment operate in environments designed for people without spending millions of dollars retrofitting the facilities.
The true test for a humanoid design is whether, if you were starting again, you would still go with a humanoid. When human compatibility is needed, the basic physical requirements stay the same: foot contact, joint torque, and wrist force.
The robots may come in different shapes, but they have the same sensory physics. Strain-based sensing endures even when the form factor changes, offering fundamental ground-truth measurement regardless of how your physical platform develops.
Deployment depth beats demo breadth
Flashy viral videos show what is technically possible. The true test, however, is not the demonstration itself but the second purchase order. Only through repeat orders can business utility be proven.
Although demonstrations using units calibrated under climate-controlled conditions prove a robot can function once, full fleet deployment demands that the robot survive at least 10,000 cycles per shift amid constant thermal variation and with near-zero tolerance for drift.
Most physical AI projects fail because the engineering effort turns instead to broad, general promises before addressing specific operational facts. In real-world situations, deployments fail due to drift, sensor fatigue, and recalibration challenges, not flaws in reasoning.
Editor’s note: Humanoids and physical AI are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.
The physical AI balance sheet
Integrating AI into physical hardware requires a disciplined balance between power consumption, thermal dissipation, mechanical wear, and safety limitations. With software, you scale by making copies; with hardware, you have to buy it, build it, and wait.
Teams that take a software approach often fail to account for this physical balance sheet. Beyond basic thermal or electrical limits, non-linear actuator gear reductions introduce complex behaviour that is notoriously difficult to predict and simulate.
True backdrivability solves part of this problem by allowing the robot actuator or joint to fully reflect any physical impact from the environment back to the core control architecture.
Whatever the hardware bottleneck may be, whether it’s thermal throttling in the joint actuators or the amount of power drawn under peak load, each constraint comes down to the same need: knowing exactly what force is present under actual loading conditions, at real temperatures, over a period of years. This is the information that strain-based sensing provides, which is why it should be included in the architecture and not just listed in the bill of materials.
The real metrics of commercial viability
To assess the commercial viability of physical AI systems, we should go beyond slick-looking marketing videos. Instead, we should focus on the metrics that finance teams actually care about.
The most important and essential metric is mean time between interventions (MTBI). This can be considered the most genuine measure used in the industry, but is the one that is least often published. If a human operator has to intervene every 20 minutes to unjam a gripper or reset a drifted sensor, then high autonomy figures have little significance.
We need to assign the same importance to the actual cost per unit of work, whether calculated on a per-pick, per meter travelled, or per inspection completed basis. This figure ultimately determines whether a robot fleet will replace or augment existing labour.
Operational value also depends on redeployment time. Deployment time shows whether a “general-purpose” platform can swiftly adjust to a new task or whether reconfiguration requires weeks of custom engineering. Lastly, the number of safety incidents per operating hour will determine if the robot ever goes outside of its cage to operate freely among human workers.
A viral video shows a robot capable of carrying out a given task once. However, a sustainable business needs the robot to carry out that same task at least 10,000 times in a row, without any intervention, drift, or failure.
The main conclusion is straightforward: Start with the workflow, build reliable sensing into the core architecture, and focus on operational metrics so both specialised machines and humanoid platforms can fulfil their potential in the physical world.
Ron Zukerman is an innovation director at Vishay Precision Group Inc. (VPG). The company is a leader in precision measurement and sensing technologies.
VPG said its sensors, weighing solutions and measurement systems optimize and enhance customers’ product performance across a broad array of markets to make the world safer, smarter, and more productive. To learn more, visit the company at www.vpgsensors.com and follow it on LinkedIn.

candidato.resumo: Mesmo após apagar uma foto, o Windows ainda pode armazenar registros do arquivo no sistema . Isso ocorre com a criação de dados temporários, mas há um caminho para removê-los rapidamente no PC. Por padrão, o Explorador de Arquivos cria miniaturas para a pré-visualização de imagens e armazena os arquivos em cache . A medida agiliza o carregamento dos resultados ao abrir a mesma pasta novamente, mas também abre uma brecha para encontrar rastros de conteúdos que já foram apagados. Vale destacar que nem toda imagem apagada ganha uma miniatura própria , mas existe um caminho para evitar a dor de cabeça e possíveis problemas com privacidade. texto_fonte:
Fotos apagadas deixam rastros perigosos no Windows; veja como eliminar tudo
Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Mesmo após apagar uma foto, o Windows ainda pode armazenar registros do arquivo no sistema. Isso ocorre com a criação de dados temporários, mas há um caminho para removê-los rapidamente no PC.
Por padrão, o Explorador de Arquivos cria miniaturas para a pré-visualização de imagens e armazena os arquivos em cache. A medida agiliza o carregamento dos resultados ao abrir a mesma pasta novamente, mas também abre uma brecha para encontrar rastros de conteúdos que já foram apagados.
Vale destacar que nem toda imagem apagada ganha uma miniatura própria, mas existe um caminho para evitar a dor de cabeça e possíveis problemas com privacidade.
Onde ficam os rastros de imagens apagadas?
Os arquivos temporários com as miniaturas ficam armazenados no caminho %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer e recebem nomes como “thumbcache_2560” (a numeração varia de acordo com a resolução da imagem).
O formato é o .db, usado para bases de dados, e não é possível acessar as imagens diretamente pelo Explorador de Arquivos — é necessário usar um software para extrair as informações.
Normalmente, as miniaturas são criadas ao abrir os arquivos pelo Explorador do Windows. Caso você delete uma imagem sem acessá-la pelo app, é possível que o sistema não gere um arquivo.
Como apagar os dados temporários no PC
Os arquivos são temporários, mas existe uma forma nativa para remover as miniaturas com a ferramenta Limpeza de Disco. Confira:
- Procure por “Limpeza de Disco” na busca e abra o app;
- Selecione a opção “Miniaturas”;
- Conclua a limpeza.

candidato.titulo: Modder discovers that putting a GPU in the 'wrong place' can deliver a 19 degree cooler hotspot
candidato.resumo: In PC DIY it might still be worth challenging convention, as TrashBench shows with his GPU hotspot getting up to 19C cooler.

texto_fonte:
It might be reasonable to assume that desktop PCs are built in a certain way due to decades of evolution and optimization. However, we're getting used to TrashBench challenging convention, and we're pleased to say the video below represents one of this enthusiast's best cooling innovations yet. In this latest video, completely ignoring the accepted norms of GPU placement delivered up to a 19°C hotspot temperature reduction but adversely impacted CPU temperatures. However, some more tweaking resulted in a 14°C reduction in hotspot temperatures and a 3.3°C cooler CPU.
TrashBench's plan was to prepare his RTX 3080 desktop PC and "test it normally, then start moving s*** around." This process began with an entirely conventional setup with the CPU cooled by a 360mm AIO, and the triple-fan RTX 3080 slotted directly into the usual PCIe expansion slot.
With the traditional build complete, TrashBench tested this baseline with a constant thermal load from looping 3DMark Time Spy and 7-Zip’s built-in benchmark. The fans in the system had their RPMs locked for consistency. Now he could start "trying to figure out if we’ve been putting the parts in the wrong place."
Beginning the first 'alternative' PC build, we heard the modder muse, "cable management isn’t important here... Is it ever?" Then we saw the GPU tested at the bottom of the case, and vertically to the side, facing one way or another, and either side of the triple case fans on the side. Meanwhile, the CPU AiO cooler was tested with the radiator fans pushing air out or bringing air in.
In summary, some configurations mostly benefitted the GPU or the CPU. But, as we noted in the intro, the sweet spot - where a worthwhile benefit was recorded in cooling both the GPU and CPU was still very worthwhile.
Taking the lessons learned from the best GPU and CPU cooling ideas, and striking a balance, TrashBench finalized his reinvented PC cooling design. That was with the CPU mounted vertically, directly against the side intake fans, and the CPU AiO cooler radiator in a traditional exhaust config. See the screenshot for the observed benefits. We’d headline this sweet spot configuration as delivering a 3.3°C cooler CPU and chilling the GPU hotspot by 14°C.
If you want to try this kind of GPU repositioning testing, a PCIe riser cable is essential. We saw TrashBench use them in a number of lengths.

texto_fonte:
5 thrillers eróticos para assistir no streaming depois de Verity
Por Jaqueline Sousa • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Verity finalmente chegou aos cinemas para fazer o público se surpreender com um mistério repleto de suspense, tensão sexual e desejo, elementos que transformaram os thrillers eróticos em um baita sucesso do formato.
Adaptação do best-seller de Colleen Hoover, Verity aposta em um elenco estelar para contar a história de Lowen (Dakota Johnson), uma escritora falida que é contratada para terminar a série literária da renomada autora Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), que sofreu um acidente que a impossibilitou de continuar a escrita.
Hospedada na luxuosa casa de Verity, Lowen logo se aproxima do marido dela, Jeremy (Josh Hartnett), descobrindo segredos sombrios da família que dificultam a sua separação entre ficção e realidade.
Melhores thrillers eróticos parecidos com Verity
Se você já assistiu Verity e gostou da atmosfera do longa-metragem, então vai gostar de saber que existem outros filmes parecidos que também podem te interessar, especialmente aqueles que misturam tensão sexual e mistérios sombrios para mexer com as emoções dos espectadores.
Pensando nisso, o Canaltech selecionou 5 thrillers eróticos para assistir no streaming depois do filme estrelado por Anne Hathaway e Dakota Johnson.
1. Instinto Selvagem (1992)
Grande expoente do movimento dos suspenses eróticos, Instinto Selvagem é um clássico do diretor Paul Verhoeven que brincou com as emoções do público nos anos 1990 ao apostar na linha tênue entre desejo e perigo, contando também com muita manipulação psicológica.
Estrelado por Michael Douglas e Sharon Stone, o filme acompanha Nick Curran (Douglas), um detetive que investiga o misterioso assassinato do namorado da engimática e sedutora escritora Catherine Tramell (Stone), cujo livro parece ter inspirado o crime. Quando a autora se torna suspeita do ocorrido, Curran se envolve em um relacionamento intenso com ela, mesmo sabendo que corre risco de vida.
Onde assistir Instinto Selvagem: Belas Arte à la Carte.
2. Observadores (2021)
Protagonizado por Sydney Sweeney, Observadores usa a curiosidade que as pessoas costumam ter com a vida dos outros para entregar um suspense repleto de mistérios. É aquele tipo de filme com reviravoltas que deixa o espectador vidrado no desenvolvimento da trama.
Dirigido por Michael Mohan, o longa conta a história de um jovem casal que começa a se interessar pela vida sexual de seus vizinhos após observá-los pela janela do apartamento. Mas a curiosidade logo se transforma em uma obsessão doentia quando ambos testemunham uma traição, fazendo com que o casal entre em um baita dilema que desencadeia uma rede de segredos obscuros.
Onde assistir Observadores: Prime Video.
3. Águas Profundas (2022)
Apostando no jogo psicológico por trás de relações complicadas, Águas Profundas pode agradar quem gostou de Verity por focar nos impactos da manipulação mental em uma relação. O longa é dirigido por Adrian Lyne, e conta com Ben Affleck, Ana de Armas e Jacob Elordi no elenco.
Na trama, um casal decide fazer um acordo para tentar salvar o casamento, com a esposa tendo a liberdade para se relacionar com outras pessoas. Contudo, esse jogo vira um pesadelo quando os amantes começam a desaparecer misteriosamente e o marido se torna o principal suspeito.
Onde assistir Águas Profundas: Prime Video e Telecine.
4. Jogo Justo (2023)
Focando nas dinâmicas de poder dentro de uma relação amorosa, Jogo Justo acompanha a jornada de um casal cujo recente noivado vira um inferno quando a mulher recebe uma promoção inesperada na firma financeira onde ambos trabalham. A partir disso, sentimentos de inveja e ressentimento surgem, transformando a relação em uma manipulação psicológica perturbadora.
Assim como Verity, Jogo Justo traz personagens moralmente duvidosos que protagonizam uma disputa de egos destrutiva, usando também o desejo como motor dessa relação conflituosa.
Onde assistir Jogo Justo: Netflix.
5. Garotas Selvagens (1998)
Dirigido por John McNaughton, Garotas Selvagens alcançou o status de clássico cult dos anos 1990 graças ao suspense erótico e às reviravoltas chocantes que permeiam sua trama. O longa ainda conta com um elenco recheado de estrelas, como Neve Campbell, Denise Richards, Kevin Bacon, Matt Dillon e Bill Murray.
Situada em uma pequena cidade costeira da Flórida, a trama conta a história de um professor que é acusado de abusar sexualmente de duas jovens estudantes. Diante da situação, um policial começa a investigar o caso, descobrindo uma perturbadora teia de mentiras, traições e interesses.
Onde assistir Garotas Selvagens: aluguel ou compra no Prime Video, Apple Tv e Google Play.
Reviravoltas emocionantes
Com tantos elementos intrigantes, Verity e os filmes citados aqui conquistam a atenção do público pela maneira como exploram os limites entre o desejo humano e dilemas morais, criando situações absurdas que mexem com as emoções do público.

candidato.titulo: Hybrid quantum computer observes foundational quantum effect in a new setting
candidato.resumo: Physicists in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford have used a hybrid quantum computer, made up of qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation. The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by traveling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.

texto_fonte:
Hybrid quantum computer observes foundational quantum effect in a new setting
Physicists in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford have used a hybrid quantum computer, made up of qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation. The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by traveling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.
The result demonstrates how hybrid quantum systems can be used to simulate interactions between matter and gauge fields that become increasingly difficult to model on classical computers. The paper has been published in Nature Physics.
A phase without crossing the field
In classical, everyday physics, the motion of a charged particle is determined locally by the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics allows a more subtle effect. In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle traveling around, rather than through, a region containing a magnetic field would still pick up a measurable trace of that field's presence. This became known as the Aharonov–Bohm effect, and it was later confirmed in experiments with real electrons.
Physicists are now interested in seeing the effect emerge in a different setting: lattice gauge theories. These are mathematical frameworks used to describe interactions between matter and gauge fields, including important models in particle and high-energy physics. In a lattice gauge theory, matter sits at the points of a grid, and the fields live on the links connecting those points.
The difficulty is that as these systems grow, their behavior becomes increasingly difficult to calculate on a classical computer. Quantum computers, which operate according to the same quantum rules the theories describe, offer another approach: Rather than solving the full dynamics on a classical computer, researchers build a physical system that behaves in the same way and observe what it does. This is known as quantum simulation.
Matter and fields share trapped ions
Beginning in 2022, lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan and colleagues in Oxford, working with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez from the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid, developed an experiment to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. Their experiment used two kinds of components, each playing a different physical role.
Qubits—quantum bits, encoded in the internal states of trapped ions—represented the gauge fields, while quantum oscillators—the vibrations of those same ions—represented the matter. Using this encoding, the team built a loop, the elementary building block of the theory, from two oscillators representing matter at two points, connected by two qubits representing the fields between them.
The team then prepared the two qubits in an entangled quantum state, in which their properties are linked in a way that has no classical equivalent. In the language of the lattice gauge theory, this corresponds to a magnetic flux piercing the loop. Producing such a flux in the conventional way, as a fixed background, would have required an interaction the hardware could not provide, so encoding it in the qubits began as a practical workaround.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics." What began as a workaround turned out to be the more interesting route.
Magnetic flux brings tunneling to a halt
The researchers then watched a matter particle tunnel around the loop. With no flux present, it tunneled freely. With the flux present, the two paths around the loop interfered destructively, suppressing the tunneling completely and leaving the system frozen in its starting state. The result was an experimental demonstration of the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a dynamical setting within a lattice gauge theory.
The paper appears alongside related work from a group at the University of Maryland led by professor Norbert Linke, which used a hybrid quantum system to simulate the Yukawa potential, an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics. The two groups developed their approaches independently before coordinating their submissions to Nature Physics. Together, the two studies highlight the potential of hybrid quantum architectures for simulating fundamental interactions that are difficult to tackle classically.
Publication details
S. Saner et al, Aharonov–Bohm interference in a Z2 lattice gauge theory on a hybrid qubit–oscillator quantum computer, Nature Physics (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03400-6
Anton T. Than et al, Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer, Nature Physics (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03402-4

candidato.titulo: Sandisk NAS 800 1.92TB SSD Review: Endurance at a premium
candidato.resumo: The Sandisk NAS 800 is a high-end PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD built for NAS workloads, with high endurance, strong sustained write performance, and low 4KB random latency. It’s mainly held back by its high price.

texto_fonte:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Sandisk NAS 800 is the premier NVMe SSD for NAS, with high endurance, high sustained write performance, and excellent 4KB random latencies, only held back by its price.
Reasons to buy
- + High TBW endurance rating
- + Exceptional sustained write performance
- + Excellent 4KB random QD1 latencies
- + Good all-around performance
Reasons to avoid
- - High price
- - Below-average power efficiency
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Sandisk is back with another welcome SSD, the NAS 800. As the name implies, this drive is designed for NAS appliances, but could also be a good choice for high-end desktop and enthusiast workstations. We recently reviewed the Optimus GX Pro 850P, a consumer drive for the PS5, so SanDisk is on a roll. The company has made it clear it wants to support the broader consumer market, as it’s even bringing back SATA SSDs in the form of the 320 and 520 series. The NAS 800 is closer in theme to the WD Red series of drives, like the WD Red SN700, which are optimized for home and small-business servers.
At its heart, the NAS 800 is a specialized, optimized Sandisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 (formerly the WD Black SN8100). That progenitor is one of the best drives on the market. It has a stellar controller and excellent all-around flash with good power efficiency and low latency. This makes a great base for a NAS drive, although some changes are necessary. The bones are good, though, and this drive could be used in any system. The only real issue is that you’re paying a premium for the NAS optimizations, and that’s where our focus is.
Sandisk NAS 800 Specifications
The Sandisk NAS 800 has some strange capacities, at least compared to consumer offerings, because the drives reserve more spare flash as overprovisioning, which improves endurance. The drive comes in 960GB, 1.92TB, 3.84TB, and 7.68TB flavors. The final one is the most welcome, as it’s been difficult to find larger drives outside of enterprise. Performance is excellent, at up to 14,900 / 13,200 MB/s for sequential reads and writes and up to 2,300K / 2,100K random read and write IOPS. Peak overall performance should be achieved at 3.84TB.
Write endurance is where this drive really stands out. It’s rated for up to 14PBW at its maximum capacity. Proportional to size, this puts it at almost three times the normal for consumer drives. The drive also supports TCG Opal self-encryption for data at rest, as would be expected for a drive in this class. Things are capped off with a standard five-year warranty.
You pay for this performance and endurance. At the time of writing,SanDisk’ss store lists the four capacities at $387.99, $699.99, $1,374.99, and $2,749.99. That’s roughly 45% to 65% more than the WD Black SN8100’s current street prices. Against the same drive under its new Optimus GX Pro 8100 name, the premium is between 27% and 29% at the time of review. The extra cost comes partly from the drive’s optimization but mostly from its TBW rating. You’re getting about one drive write per day over the five-year warranty, which is all but required for a drive of this type, and worthy of the price tag if you’re focused on endurance.
Sandisk NAS 800 Software and Accessories
If you own a Sandisk drive, or a WD drive for that matter, then you should be no stranger to the NAS 800’s software offerings. Sandisk has its own dashboard, aptly named Sandisk Dashboard, which follows the popular WD Dashboard. This SSD toolbox has all the information you need for your drive, including important SMART and health information. It also lets you enable optional features, find firmware updates, and more. Sandisk also provides a download for its OEM version of Acronis True Image, useful for backing up your files or cloning your drive.
Sandisk NAS 800: A Closer Look
The 1,920GB, or 1.92TB, version of the NAS 800 is single-sided. That also applies to the 960GB and 3.84TB versions. Only the 7.68TB version is double-sided, although that shouldn’t generally preclude you from using it in devices that would benefit from the drive. It could make a difference for certain cooling arrangements. The drive’s rating of 3.3V / 2.7A puts it at around 9W, which is between the drive’s maximum power state of 9.50W and its 6.5W / 6.4W average draw for this capacity. The reported active draw of 7.52W is higher than this average, but given that this drive is NAS-optimized with a small pseudo-SLC (pSLC) cache, it will likely be lower in practice. The drive should run cooler as a result.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The drive layout includes the SSD controller, a DRAM package, and two NAND flash packages. The 7.68TB version will need more packages on the rear, for a total of four flash packages. The controller is labeled in a way similar to SanDisk’s proprietary parts, but the “250800” spells out that this is a Silicon Motion, or SMI, SM2508. This is an eight-channel, high-end PCIe 5.0 SSD controller with generally excellent performance and power efficiency.
The DRAM package is LPDDR4 and is therefore a more power-efficient choice. It’s also 2GB, which follows the normal 1:1,000 ratio of DRAM to NAND. Our recent Optimus GX Pro 850P review had a 2TB drive from Sandisk with only 1GB of RAM. That’s perfectly suitable for gaming use. For this NAS drive, 2GB is very much preferred. The controller and DRAM are paired with SanDisk’s 218-layer BiCS8 TLC flash. This is some of the best flash on the market, with good all-around performance, very good latency, and very good power efficiency. This is world-class hardware, and the price reflects that.

candidato.titulo: CEO da Microsoft diz que IA precisa de freio controlado por humanos
candidato.resumo: CEO da Microsoft propõe controles humanos, auditorias independentes e mecanismos de contenção para evitar que modelos avançados de inteligência artificial executem ações sem supervisão O post CEO da Microsoft diz que IA precisa de freio controlado por humanos apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

texto_fonte:
Satya Nadella, presidente do conselho e CEO da Microsoft, defendeu em uma publicação no X neste sábado (10) que sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) tenham mecanismos de contenção e um botão de emergência controlado por humanos. A proposta prevê que pessoas autorizadas possam interromper ou desligar um modelo durante a execução de uma tarefa, como parte de uma estrutura de segurança para tecnologias capazes de acessar dados sensíveis e realizar operações importantes.
O executivo argumenta que empresas não devem depender apenas das garantias oferecidas pelos desenvolvedores de IA. Em vez disso, precisam estabelecer limites de acesso, monitorar as ações dos modelos e manter controles externos que permitam intervir quando necessário. As recomendações foram apresentadas em meio a alertas de executivos e pesquisadores sobre os riscos associados ao avanço da tecnologia e à insuficiência de mecanismos de segurança.
https://t.co/MjwFy73LOF
— Satya Nadella (@satyanadella) October 10, 2026
Microsoft propõe novos controles para sistemas de IA
Na publicação, Satya Nadella afirma que os modelos atuais não permitem compreender completamente como determinadas respostas e comportamentos são produzidos. Segundo ele, diferentemente dos softwares tradicionais, nem sempre é possível relacionar as ações de um modelo a entradas específicas dos dados de treinamento ou a configurações dos parâmetros internos.
O CEO defende que sistemas de IA sejam tratados como possíveis riscos internos às organizações, não necessariamente por serem maliciosos, mas porque podem cometer erros ou ser comprometidos quando têm acesso a recursos importantes. A abordagem proposta prevê a separação entre o modelo e a estrutura responsável por organizar sua execução, além da definição externa das ações que ele pode realizar.
Nadella também afirma que os controles de segurança não devem ficar sob responsabilidade do próprio modelo. Na avaliação do executivo, as organizações precisam ter autonomia para determinar quais informações podem ser acessadas e quais operações podem ser executadas, sem permitir que a IA altere ou contorne as regras estabelecidas.
Sete princípios para aumentar a segurança da IA
O executivo apresentou uma série de princípios para orientar o desenvolvimento e a operação de sistemas avançados. A lista inclui a utilização de modelos diferentes para tarefas importantes, o registro verificável das ações realizadas e a realização contínua de testes que contemplem falhas, ataques e situações extremas.
Outro ponto é a auditabilidade independente. Para Satya Nadella, a validação de um sistema não deve depender exclusivamente da mesma inteligência artificial que está sendo avaliada. A proposta também prevê que cada ação relevante deixe registros legíveis por humanos e protegidos contra alterações, permitindo reconstruir como determinado resultado foi alcançado.
O princípio de contenção estabelece que as empresas devem partir do pressuposto de que um modelo pode estar comprometido. Por isso, uma pessoa autorizada precisa conseguir pausar ou desligar o sistema durante uma tarefa. Nadella acrescenta que modelos mais avançados exigirão tecnologias de contenção mais sofisticadas, que deverão ser padronizadas.
A lista inclui ainda a divulgação rápida de incidentes às partes afetadas. Quando um sistema falhar ou for comprometido, as organizações deverão informar o ocorrido, explicar quais mecanismos de controle falharam e compartilhar aprendizados que ajudem a prevenir novos problemas.
Executivos alertam para os riscos do avanço da IA
As declarações de Satya Nadella ocorrem em meio a discussões sobre a velocidade de desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial e a necessidade de ampliar as medidas de segurança. Entre os nomes que já se manifestaram sobre o tema estão Bill Gates, cofundador da Microsoft, Dario Amodei, CEO da Anthropic, Sam Altman, CEO da OpenAI, e Elon Musk, CEO da SpaceX.
Em setembro, Amodei defendeu uma desaceleração no desenvolvimento de sistemas avançados de IA. Segundo as informações reunidas pela CNBC, a proposta recebeu apoio de Altman e Musk. Pesquisadores também manifestaram preocupação com os riscos da tecnologia e com a capacidade das empresas de manter o controle sobre seus modelos.
A posição contrasta com a do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, que tem rejeitado alertas sobre possíveis riscos de extinção relacionados à IA e enfatizado a necessidade de manter o país à frente da China no setor. Em outubro, o governo Trump também apresentou uma iniciativa chamada AI Force, liderada pelo diretor de Inteligência Nacional, Jay Clayton, com o objetivo de facilitar as atividades do setor e identificar agentes mal-intencionados.
Para Nadella, a segurança não deve depender da confiança depositada em um modelo específico. O executivo defende uma arquitetura na qual os sistemas possam ser observados, testados e limitados por mecanismos independentes, permitindo que as organizações mantenham o controle sobre as ações executadas em seu nome.

candidato.titulo: Scientists may have found a shortcut to fusion energy
candidato.resumo: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory may have found a dramatically more efficient route to fusion energy by reversing the traditional approach: heating plasma first, then increasing its density. Their calculations could help future reactors reach self-sustaining fusion with far less energy while avoiding hidden problems that make ignition harder.

texto_fonte:
Scientists may have found a shortcut to fusion energy
Scientists have uncovered a potentially far more efficient path to fusion ignition that could bring the dream of practical fusion energy closer to reality.
- Date:
- October 10, 2026
- Source:
- Princeton University
- Summary:
- Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory may have found a dramatically more efficient route to fusion energy by reversing the traditional approach: heating plasma first, then increasing its density. Their calculations could help future reactors reach self-sustaining fusion with far less energy while avoiding hidden problems that make ignition harder.
- Share:
Scientists at the U.S.Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) have identified a potentially much more efficient way to achieve fusion ignition, a major milestone in the pursuit of practical fusion energy. Their calculations suggest that changing the order in which plasma is heated and compressed could dramatically reduce the energy needed to reach a self-sustaining fusion reaction.
For more than seven decades, fusion researchers have relied on a mathematical rule to determine whether plasma can remain sufficiently hot and dense, for a long enough period, to sustain fusion without additional external heating. Known as the Lawson criterion, this equation defines the conditions required for ignition. However, it does not explain the most efficient way to achieve them.
Now, PPPL physicists Luis Delgado-Aparicio, Masayuki Ono, and Jonathan Menard have developed a more comprehensive version of the criterion. By incorporating four additional factors that influence fusion performance, they have mapped a promising route to ignition that could require substantially less energy than alternative approaches.
Their findings were published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
The research focuses on plasma, often called the fourth state of matter. Plasma forms when a gas becomes so energetic that its particles carry electrical charges. In fusion reactors, this extremely hot material contains the atomic nuclei that researchers hope to combine, releasing energy through nuclear fusion.
The ultimate goal is to produce a burning plasma, in which fusion reactions generate enough heat to sustain the process without continued external heating. Reaching this state efficiently remains one of the most important challenges in fusion energy research.
Scientists Find a Shortcut to Fusion Ignition
Delgado-Aparicio compares the discovery to finding a more efficient route through a mountain range.
Imagine that the energy requirements for fusion ignition form a landscape dominated by a towering mountain. The destination lies on the other side, but there are several possible routes to reach it.
Many proposed fusion strategies effectively attempt to climb directly over the mountain. They begin by increasing the density of the plasma and then supplying the enormous amount of heat needed to reach ignition.
The new calculations suggest that a different sequence could be considerably more efficient. Instead of increasing density first, researchers could heat the plasma before making it denser. This alternative route avoids the highest energy requirements while still reaching the desired conditions.
"A lot of companies want to climb the mountain head-on and spend enormous energy to get there," Delgado-Aparicio said. "Go around the peak instead. You reach the same place in a much smarter way, and you use far less energy."
The Hidden Mountain Pass in Fusion Physics
The researchers identified a particularly important region of this mathematical landscape called the Cordey saddle.
In geographical terms, a saddle is a low passage between higher elevations. In fusion physics, the Cordey saddle represents a relatively accessible point along the boundary separating plasma that still needs outside heating from plasma capable of sustaining its own fusion reactions.
To evaluate different routes, the scientists used a measurement called Q, which compares the power produced by fusion reactions with the external heating power supplied to the plasma.
For example, a Q value of 5 means the fusion reactions produce five times as much power as the external heating system delivers.
In an idealized plasma containing only pure fusion fuel, the Cordey saddle occurs at approximately Q = 5. However, actual fusion systems are much more complicated. Contaminants within the plasma and extremely strong magnetic fields can shift the location of this passage, increasing the Q value needed to reach it.
Understanding how these conditions change is essential for determining whether a proposed fusion reactor can realistically achieve ignition.
A More Realistic Roadmap for Future Fusion Reactors
The findings could influence the design of two major types of magnetic fusion devices: tokamaks and stellarators.
Both approaches use powerful magnetic fields to confine plasma while it is heated to the extraordinary temperatures needed for fusion. Tokamaks, which have a characteristic doughnut shape, are among the leading technologies being investigated for future fusion power plants.
Research institutions and private companies are pursuing several different ways to generate electricity from fusion and eventually deliver that power to the electrical grid. Identifying an efficient route to ignition could help engineers design more practical systems while avoiding costly mistakes.
For PPPL, this work is part of a broader effort to address the scientific and technological challenges that must be overcome before commercial fusion power becomes possible, including the development of future fusion pilot plants.
One of the study's major advances is that it evaluates several important physical processes together rather than examining them separately, as much previous research has done.
The researchers incorporated four additional factors that can influence whether a plasma reaches and maintains ignition:
- Helium ash buildup: Fusion reactions produce helium as a byproduct. As this spent fuel accumulates, it can dilute the remaining fusion fuel and reduce performance.
- Plasma contamination: Light and heavy impurities can enter the plasma from materials lining the inside of the reactor, interfering with fusion conditions.
- Synchrotron radiation: Electrons traveling through magnetic fields emit radiation, carrying energy away from the plasma.
- Heat loss: Energy continuously escapes from the plasma, and these losses can become greater as its temperature rises.
Accounting for these effects produces a more realistic picture of the conditions future reactors must achieve.
"When you leave these effects out, you say the design will work fine," Ono said. "When you put them in, the picture changes, and it becomes quite important."
According to Ono, the goal is to establish a more reliable, widely applicable model that scientists can use to evaluate fusion reactor designs before construction begins.
Treating the Lawson criterion as a single unchanging threshold overlooks physical processes that can substantially alter the requirements for ignition. Including those effects early in the design process could prevent expensive problems later.
"Fusion experiments cost a great deal of money, and you do not want to make mistakes you could have caught beforehand," he said.
Tiny Amounts of Tungsten Could Make Fusion Much Harder
One particularly striking finding concerns tungsten, an extremely heat-resistant metal selected for the interior walls of more than a dozen next-generation fusion machines.
Tungsten is attractive because fusion reactors must withstand conditions involving plasma temperatures greater than those found at the center of the sun. However, the material also presents a significant challenge if even tiny quantities enter the plasma.
The team's calculations show that tungsten contamination at a concentration of just one part in 10,000 can approximately double the pressure required to achieve fusion ignition.
That is a substantial increase caused by an exceptionally small amount of material.
The calculations were initially developed in two dimensions. When the researchers extended their analysis to three dimensions, they found that the pressure needed for ignition could exceed the limits at which the plasma remains stable.
This suggests that seemingly minor contamination could have major consequences for the feasibility of certain fusion reactor designs.
How Energy Losses Could Help Stabilize Fusion
Surprisingly, some of the processes that make ignition more difficult may also help fusion reactors operate more safely and consistently.
Scientists have long investigated the possibility of thermal "runaway" instability. This occurs when heat from fusion reactions increases the reaction rate, producing still more heat and potentially creating a self-reinforcing cycle.
The researchers found that energy losses within the plasma can naturally counteract this effect.
Although those losses increase the difficulty of reaching ignition, they also provide a balancing influence that could allow a burning plasma to maintain a stable operating state without constant adjustments.
This balance could be valuable for future reactor designs.
(Unlike a fission power plant, a fusion system holds only seconds of fuel at a time, so losing control means the plasma cools and the burn stops rather than anything worse.)
Liquid Lithium and Advanced Fuel Could Improve Fusion Efficiency
The study also identifies technologies that might help overcome some of the obstacles revealed by the calculations.
One possibility involves coating the inside of fusion reactors with liquid lithium, a technique PPPL researchers have investigated for years.
These coatings could help prevent tungsten from entering the plasma while reducing heat losses, making it easier to maintain the extreme conditions necessary for fusion.
Another promising approach uses spin-polarized fuel. This involves preparing the atomic nuclei so that their spins are aligned before fusion occurs, which can increase the fusion reaction rate.
Together, these strategies could improve the performance of future reactors and make the path to ignition more achievable.
What Comes Next for the New Fusion Strategy?
Despite the promising findings, the proposed heat-first approach has not yet been demonstrated experimentally.
The research is theoretical and relies on mathematical calculations rather than direct measurements. Existing fusion experiments have not reached the temperatures associated with the Cordey saddle, preventing scientists from testing the predicted route under those conditions.
The PPPL team plans to investigate the approach further through digital experiments, using computer-based simulations to explore whether heating plasma before increasing its density can deliver the expected advantages.
If future studies confirm the calculations, the findings could provide an important foundation for designing more efficient fusion systems and help researchers make better decisions about reactor construction.
"While more study is needed, we are excited by these results, and they suggest a clear path forward for future research in this area," said Menard.
The work was supported by the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences, under contract DE-AC02-09CH11466. Additional support came through a 2015 Fusion Energy Sciences Early Career Award, a 2018 Diagnostic Innovation and Development award, and the 2021 and 2025 Long-Pulse Tokamak Research Programs.

O que é root no Android?
Por Viviane França • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Muitos usuários do Android consideram fazer root para ter mais controle sobre o celular e acessar recursos que ficam limitados pelas fabricantes ou operadoras. O procedimento costuma ser procurado por quem quer remover aplicativos pré-instalados, personalizar a interface ou modificar funções do sistema que não estão disponíveis na configuração de fábrica.
Embora o Android tenha componentes de código aberto, as fabricantes aplicam restrições e permissões para proteger o sistema e os dados do usuário. O root altera essas limitações e concede privilégios elevados de administração, conhecidos como acesso de superusuário.
Esse acesso abre novas possibilidades de personalização, mas também modifica o modelo de segurança do Android. Por isso, fazer root envolve riscos que devem ser considerados, como perda de suporte da fabricante, exposição maior a malwares e a possibilidade de inutilizar o aparelho em caso de erro durante o processo.
A seguir, confira:
- O que é root no Android?
- Qual é a diferença entre root e jailbreak?
- Qual é a diferença entre root e bootloader?
- Quais são os riscos e benefícios de fazer root no Android?
O que é root no Android?
Fazer root no Android é obter privilégios de superusuário no sistema. Com esse acesso, o usuário pode modificar arquivos, configurações e componentes que normalmente ficam protegidos pelo aparelho.
Para entender o que muda com o root, é preciso considerar como o Android controla o acesso ao sistema. O sistema utiliza o kernel do Linux, que trabalha com diferentes níveis de permissão. No uso normal, o aparelho restringe o acesso a arquivos e áreas importantes, tanto para o usuário quanto para os aplicativos. Já o superusuário, ou root, tem privilégios elevados para executar comandos e modificar partes protegidas do sistema.
Essas restrições existem, entre outros motivos, para impedir que um aplicativo interfira no funcionamento de outro. O Android utiliza a sandbox, um ambiente isolado no qual os aplicativos funcionam. Dessa forma, um programa não consegue acessar livremente os dados de outro ou alterar arquivos essenciais do sistema.
O root reduz essas limitações para aplicativos que recebem autorização de superusuário. Com mais liberdade para acessar o sistema, o usuário pode fazer modificações que não seriam possíveis em um aparelho sem root. Ao mesmo tempo, um erro ou aplicativo malicioso com esse nível de acesso também pode causar problemas mais graves.
Qual é a diferença entre root e jailbreak?
Root e jailbreak têm uma proposta parecida: dar ao usuário mais liberdade para modificar o sistema do aparelho. A diferença está na plataforma em que cada procedimento é usado e no tipo de restrição que ele remove.
No Android, o root concede privilégios de superusuário e libera o acesso a áreas que ficam protegidas no uso comum. Com essas permissões, o usuário pode modificar arquivos do sistema e usar ferramentas que dependem de acesso elevado.
No iPhone e iPad, o jailbreak tem uma função semelhante, mas está ligado às restrições do iOS e do iPadOS. O procedimento pode liberar a execução de códigos e a instalação de recursos que não são autorizados normalmente pela Apple.
Qual é a diferença entre root e bootloader?
O root não é a mesma coisa que desbloquear o bootloader. Os dois procedimentos podem fazer parte de um processo de modificação do aparelho, mas têm funções distintas.
O bootloader é o programa responsável por iniciar o sistema operacional quando o celular é ligado. Por padrão, ele verifica se o software instalado no aparelho está autorizado a ser executado. Ao desbloquear o bootloader, essa restrição é removida, o que abre caminho para alterações mais profundas no software, como a instalação de uma ROM customizada. O procedimento, por si só, não concede privilégios de superusuário.
Já o root atua dentro do sistema operacional e amplia as permissões disponíveis para o usuário e para aplicativos autorizados. Por isso, é possível desbloquear o bootloader sem fazer root, dependendo do tipo de modificação que se pretende realizar.
Quais são os riscos e benefícios de fazer root no Android?
O principal benefício do root é ampliar o controle sobre o aparelho. Entre as possibilidades estão:
- Personalização profunda: alteração de elementos da interface, fontes, ícones, animações, notificações e outros componentes do sistema;
- Remoção de aplicativos pré-instalados: exclusão de determinados programas da fabricante ou da operadora que não podem ser desinstalados normalmente;
- Alteração de parâmetros do aparelho: em dispositivos compatíveis, algumas ferramentas permitem modificar parâmetros do processador e da GPU;
- Automação: uso de aplicativos que precisam de privilégios elevados para executar determinadas tarefas;
- Alteração de arquivos do sistema: acesso a áreas protegidas que não ficam disponíveis para aplicativos comuns;
- Backups mais completos: possibilidade de usar ferramentas capazes de acessar partes do sistema que normalmente ficam protegidas.
Essa liberdade, porém, vem acompanhada de riscos que podem afetar o funcionamento, a segurança e o suporte do aparelho:
- Brick: erros durante a modificação ou instalação de arquivos do sistema podem fazer o aparelho deixar de inicializar ou funcionar corretamente. Em casos mais graves, o celular pode ficar inutilizável;
- Garantia e suporte: o root pode afetar a garantia ou o suporte oferecido pela fabricante, dependendo do aparelho, da região e do tipo de problema apresentado. A modificação também pode causar dificuldades para instalar ou receber atualizações oficiais;
- Riscos de segurança: ao conceder privilégios de superusuário, o usuário amplia o que aplicativos autorizados a usar root podem fazer no aparelho. Um malware com esse nível de acesso pode tentar acessar informações, modificar arquivos, instalar programas ou alterar configurações importantes;
- Aplicativos incompatíveis: bancos, carteiras digitais, jogos competitivos e serviços de streaming podem detectar alterações no sistema e restringir determinadas funções por motivos de segurança;
- Danos ao hardware: alterações inadequadas nos parâmetros de desempenho podem causar aquecimento excessivo, aumentar o consumo de energia e acelerar o desgaste da bateria. Dependendo da modificação, recursos, como câmera e leitor de impressão digital, também podem deixar de funcionar corretamente.
Por esses motivos, o root costuma fazer mais sentido para desenvolvedores e usuários avançados que entendem as consequências das alterações e sabem como recuperar o aparelho caso algo dê errado. Para quem usa o celular no dia a dia, os riscos podem superar as vantagens de ter acesso de superusuário.
